comparison: Both evaluate ChIP-seq co-localization data (C3-C10). OpenEval finds the evidence SUPPORTED and interprets close binding as indicating complex formation or close association. Peer reviewers rate this UNCERTAIN, explicitly challenging the complex formation interpretation without co-immunoprecipitation evidence, stating 'this is an unfounded claim' without proof of physical interaction.

OpenEval R1 addresses ChIP-seq experimental design and validation (C1, C2, C68-C70). Peer R1 partially overlaps on C1-C2 but focuses on challenging the complex formation interpretation. OpenEval finds the methodology well-justified (SUPPORTED), while peer reviewers question the interpretation despite acknowledging the data as valuable.

OpenEval R3 covers RNA-seq results (C11-C14, C71). Peer R2 includes these claims plus BETA analysis (C15-C21). Both find the RNA-seq data SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm the findings, with one stating the data shows SMA-3 as activator and SMA-9 with dual function.

Both evaluate BETA analysis and transcriptional function interpretation (C15-C21). OpenEval finds the activator/dual function conclusions SUPPORTED based on regulatory patterns. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, explicitly affirming 'all SMA-3-controlled targets are positively controlled' and acknowledging SMA-9's dual function, though noting SMA-9's function 'remains obscure.'

Both evaluate the LOA/BETA integration for identifying co-regulated targets (C22-C26). OpenEval finds the sophisticated analytical approach SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, acknowledging the findings without challenge and describing the analysis as 'valuable' and 'extremely useful for the community.'

Both address factor-exclusive targets (C27-C30). OpenEval finds the identification of exclusive targets and SMA-9's dual function SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, summarizing the findings including the curious observation of opposing regulation by the two factors.

Perfect overlap on HOT site analysis (C31-C33). Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the analysis addresses non-specific binding concerns and finds most functional sites are not at HOT sites. Peer reviewers accept this without challenge as part of the valuable ChIP-seq characterization.

Both evaluate genetic interaction data showing intermediate phenotypes (C34-C35). OpenEval R8 also includes C90. Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the data challenges simple epistasis models. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm the epistasis finding, stating 'SMA-9 appears to act epistatically to SMA-3.'

Both address qRT-PCR validation of epistatic relationships (C36-C38). Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the double mutant phenotypes support epistasis across multiple genes. Peer reviewers acknowledge this data as evidence for SMA-9's epistatic action without challenge.

Perfect overlap on GO term enrichment analysis (C39-C42). Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the analysis reveals convergent and factor-specific functions consistent with overlapping/exclusive targets. Peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge the GO findings, particularly regarding cuticle collagen synthesis regulation.

Both evaluate functional validation through body size measurements (C43-C44, C72). OpenEval R11 focuses on systematic RNAi screening methodology. Peer R7 includes additional claims about dpy-11 (C45-C47). Both rate SUPPORTED, treating the functional screening as validating the transcriptional target identification.

Both address dpy-11 as key downstream effector (C45-C47). Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the severe phenotype and differential regulation by SMA-3. Peer reviewers acknowledge dpy-11 as an important direct target of SMA-3 regulating cuticle development.

Both evaluate collagen secretion defects (C48-C51). OpenEval R13 focuses on the finding that secretion rather than expression is affected. Peer R8 includes additional ER microscopy claims (C52-C54). Both rate SUPPORTED, with peer reviewers providing 'compelling evidence' for the secretion mechanism.

Both address high-resolution microscopy evidence for secretion defects (C52-C53). Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes ER colocalization and altered morphology as mechanistic support. Peer reviewers accept this as part of the compelling evidence for BMP-dependent collagen secretion defects.

Strong overlap on ER secretion defect evidence (C54-C58). Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes convergence of genetic and pharmacological perturbations. Peer reviewers describe this as 'compelling evidence' for the collagen secretion mechanism, accepting the tunicamycin and vesicle transport experiments.

Both evaluate the main mechanistic conclusion about ER-mediated collagen secretion (C59, C97). OpenEval R16 includes additional synthesis claims (C92-C96). Both rate SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm this as 'compelling evidence' for BMP-dependent body size control through collagen secretion defects.

Both address experimental design and validation (C68-C70). OpenEval R1 also includes ChIP-seq peak identification (C1-C2). Peer R11 includes C71 (known target validation). Both rate SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers implicitly accept the experimental approach by describing datasets as 'valuable' and 'extremely useful.'

Minimal overlap on validation of known targets (C71). Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval treats this as confirmation of the RNA-seq approach. Peer reviewers accept this as appropriate validation without challenge.

OpenEval R17 evaluates background knowledge claims (C60-C67, C79-C89, C91) appropriately cited to prior literature. Rated SUPPORTED as established context. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as peer reviewers focused on novel findings rather than background claims.

OpenEval R18 evaluates background on metabolic and ECM biology (C73-C78) that contextualizes findings. Rated SUPPORTED as appropriately cited established facts. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as peer reviewers did not separately evaluate background contextual claims.
